slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by framing neutral geometry as the chapter where the course asks what remains true before choosing any parallel postulate. The visible source span anchors the lecture, but the mathematical promise is local: SAS, angle measure, congruence, right triangles, and tangent tests are enough to build a surprisingly large proof machine.

slides.title: Route
slides.notes: Use the route slide as a dependency chart, not merely a table of contents. Students should see that SAS is the gate that unlocks congruence, exterior-angle inequalities, right-triangle reasoning, and circle theorems. Keep emphasizing the audit question: did the argument quietly smuggle in a Euclidean parallel fact, or does it survive in any neutral model?

slides.title: Neutral Stance
slides.notes: Pause on the word neutral and make it operational. The point is not vagueness; it is discipline. We are allowed to measure segments and angles, use separation, and invoke SAS. We are not allowed to use similarity, angle sums equal to two right angles, or unique parallels unless they have already been proved without the parallel postulate.

slides.title: SAS
slides.notes: Treat SAS as the chapter's first real lever. The diagram is deliberately an overlay: after the two side lengths and the included angle are matched, the second triangle has no remaining freedom. Invite students to say exactly which data are used and which conclusions are earned, because that habit prevents circular congruence proofs later.

slides.title: Triangle Toolkit
slides.notes: Present the toolbox as derived technology. Students often memorize names of congruence tests without noticing that each test has to be paid for by earlier neutral facts. The table gives a practical reading: every time a proof says triangles are congruent, identify the entry data, the neutral move that converts it, and the part being transported.

slides.title: Exterior Angle
slides.notes: Use this theorem as the first major place where the no-parallel rule matters. In Euclidean geometry students may instinctively subtract from one hundred eighty degrees, but that is not neutral. The neutral proof instead builds a comparison triangle and uses congruence plus betweenness to force the exterior angle to dominate the remote interior angles.

slides.title: Inequalities
slides.notes: Move slowly from theorem to consequences. The point is that neutral geometry can compare sizes without using similarity or coordinate slope. The exterior-angle theorem supplies the contradiction pattern: assume the wrong order, construct a comparison point or triangle, and watch an angle become both larger and not larger than another angle.

slides.title: Right Triangles
slides.notes: Right triangles are useful because perpendicularity adds a rigid angle for free. Emphasize that the hypotenuse-leg pattern is not a new magic axiom; it is a compressed congruence argument. The proof strategy is often to introduce an auxiliary perpendicular, prove two right triangles congruent, and then read off the hidden equality or angle relation.

slides.title: Perpendicular Bisectors
slides.notes: Use this slide to show a typical neutral proof template in miniature. A locus statement sounds global, but the proof is local: introduce the midpoint, draw the perpendicular, and compare the two right triangles. This is also a good moment to ask students which direction of the statement is easier and why the converse needs care.

slides.title: Tangents
slides.notes: Connect circle geometry back to right triangles. The radius to the tangency point supplies the perpendicular, and the perpendicular supplies a shortest-distance comparison. The converse is equally important for constructions: once a radius is known, the perpendicular through the point gives the only possible tangent line at that point.

slides.title: Tangent Workflow
slides.notes: This workflow is meant to make circle proofs less mystical. A tangent proof has obligations: put the point on the circle, establish a perpendicular radius, compare every other point on the line by right-triangle logic, and only then claim single contact. That order is what turns a convincing drawing into a neutral theorem.

slides.title: Proof Flow
slides.notes: Use the graph to normalize proof bookkeeping. A neutral proof is not just a linear paragraph; it is a dependency structure. When students struggle, ask them to name the node they need next: a definition to make an object legal, an axiom to start a construction, a lemma to move equality, or a model check to test intuition.

slides.title: Model Checks
slides.notes: Explain why the computational checks belong in a proof-heavy chapter. They are not empirical substitutes for theorem proofs, but they help students inspect whether a constructed figure is meaningful. The chapter checks record betweenness, nonzero area, angle measurement, visual variation, and artifact count so the diagrams remain accountable to geometry rather than decoration.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter question: how much geometry works before choosing a parallel axiom? The answer is more than students expect. A neutral proof can establish robust triangle congruence, inequality, right-triangle, and tangent facts. The exit problems ask students to practice the method, not to recite theorem names.
